summary: This Best Current Practice sets a policy for moderating disruptive participation across the IETF's public mailing lists and other discussion channels. It sets guardrails for moderation and creates a moderator team that will develop procedures and apply them consistently alongside chairs and administrators. It obsoletes RFC 3683 and RFC 3934 and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 9245.

eli5.summary: When kids in a club keep shouting and ruining it for others, the club picks a few helpers with clear rules to calmly stop it.

subtitle: How the IETF handles disruptive behavior on its mailing lists, chats and other public forums.

tldr.problem: The IETF's older moderation tools were inconsistent and slow: each chair or list administrator applied their own criteria to a single list, and the community-wide posting-rights action was cumbersome and rarely used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9945 creates an IETF moderator team, appointed by the IESG, that develops public moderation procedures and works with chairs and administrators, with guardrails, transparency rules and an appeals path.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3683 and RFC 3934 and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 9245. The changes take effect once the IESG approves the procedures in Section 4.

facts.label: Reinstatement request
facts.value: No earlier than a year after the decision, then annually

today: RFC 9945 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 245) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 3683 and RFC 3934 and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 9245, with effect once the IESG approves the procedures in Section 4.

sections.title: Purpose and Philosophy
sections.content:
RFC 9945 sets a policy for moderating disruptive participation across the IETF's public online channels and creates a moderator team to develop procedures and help apply them consistently. The abstract sums up the tone: the IETF will treat people with kindness and grace, but not endless patience.

Disagreement is expected and healthy in a discussion-based rough consensus process. Engaged, respectful discussion within the scope of a forum is not disruptive, and nobody is disruptive solely because they are outside the rough consensus. Even so, when someone crosses into disruptive behavior, action must be taken to maintain decorum.

The goals are consistent, fair and timely moderation regardless of a person's role or past technical contributions; available appeals; a balance of transparency against privacy; decisions that can be reconsidered; and the broadest possible latitude for moderators. The objective is explicitly not punishment, but an open, welcoming, non-hostile environment where all participate on an equal footing.

The policy applies to IETF activities only, not to bodies such as the IRTF, the IAB or the Independent RFC Submission Stream without their explicit agreement.
sections.eli5: People may disagree, and that is fine. But if someone keeps being disruptive, the club steps in. The goal is to keep it friendly for everybody, not to punish.

sections.title: What It Replaces
sections.content:
The memo changes earlier processes in four ways. It obsoletes RFC 3683, because the "posting rights" action it defines is replaced by the new processes. It obsoletes RFC 3934, which it replaces as the working group moderation procedure. It obsoletes Section 3 and the second paragraph of Section 4 of RFC 9245, because the new team replaces the IETF discussion list moderator team. And it updates Section 6.1 of RFC 2418, since the moderator team will work with working group chairs.

These changes take effect when the procedures described in Section 4 have been approved by the IESG. Until those procedures exist, all previous processes remain in effect.
sections.eli5: The new team takes over jobs that older rules gave to other people, but the old rules stay until the new ones are ready.

sections.title: The Moderator Team and Its Roles
sections.content:
The IESG appoints and recalls moderators. The team starts with no fewer than five people and may grow or shrink with experience. The IESG weighs geographic coverage, absences and diversity, and the team should cover time zones so it can ideally respond within a few hours. Current IESG or IAB members cannot be moderators, because those bodies sit in the appeals chain. Members of other NomCom-appointed bodies, such as the IETF Trust or IETF LLC Board, and IETF LLC staff and contractors are also excluded.

Responsibilities are shared. Participants should behave as described in Section 1.2 and report disruption to a forum administrator and the moderators. Administrators, who are working group chairs by default, manage their forums and must address reports promptly. Moderators set procedures and may act when administrators do not respond or when someone disrupts several forums at once; they first try to contact and advise the administrators and must notify them of any action. Moderators are administrators of IETF plenary forums such as the discussion and Last Call lists. Area directors resolve conflicts and the IESG oversees the team without running it day to day.

The IETF commits to providing or funding training for administrators and moderators.
sections.eli5: Everyone has a part. Members report problems, the people running each group handle them first, and the helper team steps in if they cannot or if the trouble spreads to many groups.

sections.title: Procedures, Transparency and Reinstatement
sections.content:
The moderator team's first task is to develop procedures and criteria with community input. These must be approved by the IESG before they take effect and be made public, though they need not be written as RFCs. The intent is wide freedom of action with the minimal necessary actions taken. Anyone told to stop disrupting a forum must stop immediately. Listed examples, which are not prescriptive, include automated rate limiting, review and approval of messages, a private or public admonishment, and temporary or indefinite suspension of participation privileges.

Any action restricting participation privileges is reported at once to the affected person, the relevant administrators and the moderator team, and periodically to the IESG. Suspensions longer than fourteen days must also be reported to the affected forum, and moderators periodically publish an aggregate report to the community.

Someone indefinitely suspended may request reinstatement no earlier than a year after the decision, and then only annually. The deciding party may reinstate conditionally or unconditionally. Refusals cannot be appealed, to avoid denial-of-service attacks on IETF processes, and reinstatement is described as a grace, not a right.
sections.eli5: The helpers write down the rules in public and tell people when they are limited. A person who has been stopped for good can ask to come back after a year, but nobody is promised a yes.

sections.title: Scope and Out-of-Scope Actions
sections.content:
The policy covers all public online IETF forums, present and future: mailing lists, chat groups and systems such as shared code repositories, wikis or issue trackers. Moderator actions are permitted only to limit disruptive communication in online forums. Out-of-scope examples include Datatracker account removal, restricting in-person, virtual or hybrid meeting participation, content removal or redaction, and policing private or non-IETF communications.

Unsolicited bulk messages are treated as disruptive and handled under the IESG statement on spam control or its successors, with no extra reporting needed. Appendix B gives non-normative examples of disruption, among them off-topic discussion, uncivil commentary, unsanctioned event announcements, repeatedly arguing against an IESG-approved WG charter and "sealioning", which is incessant requests for evidence while staying superficially polite. The RFC stresses that moderation involves subjective judgment and that no list can be complete.
sections.eli5: The helpers deal with messy behavior in public online spaces. They cannot delete accounts or keep people out of meetings, and junk mail is handled by the spam rules.

sections.title: Appeals and Other IETF Functions
sections.content:
Anyone can take a disagreement over a moderation decision to the responsible area director, or to the IETF Chair if none can be determined. If the area director cannot resolve it, the matter may go to the IESG and then the IAB under Sections 6.5.1 and 6.5.4 of RFC 2026.

The moderators complement the IETF Ombudsteam, whose focus on anti-harassment is unchanged, and should always report suspected harassment while still acting on disruptive behavior. The IETF LLC Board has a fiduciary duty that includes protecting the organization from serious legal risk. In rare cases, on legal advice, it may take emergency moderation actions, for example against a credible threat of harm or of legal action. It should inform the IESG, the moderators and the community unless legal advice says otherwise. Such actions cannot be overridden by the moderator team or the IESG, are outside the rest of the policy, and can be reviewed by the LLC Board.
sections.eli5: If you think a decision was unfair, you can ask the next person up, step by step. There is also a rare emergency route for serious legal danger.

sections.title: Risks of Abuse
sections.content: The RFC says the usual security considerations do not apply. The risk it names is abuse of moderation by moderators, chairs or others, leading to censorship of legitimate participation. It lists eight mitigations: uniform procedures to be set first; the statement that views outside the rough consensus are not disruptive in themselves; immediate reporting of restrictive actions to those affected and to the moderators, and periodic reports to the IESG; community notice of suspensions beyond 14 days; the appeals process; the ability to update procedures with community input and IESG approval; the option to comment to the NomCom or community if the IESG or IAB fail in oversight; and the fact that the policy itself may be amended.
sections.eli5: Helpers could misuse their power, so the rules add checks: be open about what happens, allow appeals, and let the community change the rules if they stop working.

sections.title: Why the Old Approach Fell Short
sections.content:
Appendix A explains the background. Chairs moderated working group meetings under RFC 2418 and mailing lists under RFC 3934, IESG statements guided other lists, and the general discussion list had its own moderators. RFC 3683 let the IESG propose revoking an individual's posting rights after a community Last Call.

The RFC lists the problems. There was no agreed definition of disruptive behavior, so criteria varied. The RFC 3934 process was slow and assumed a misguided participant who could be reasoned with. Chairs could act only on their own list, even when disruption spanned several. Posting-rights actions were cumbersome, slow and inconsistent, rarely used and seen as heavy-handed. Participants might not feel comfortable reporting to a chair or an anonymous list alias. And processes existed only for in-person meetings and mailing lists, not for chat, wikis, virtual meetings or code repositories.
sections.eli5: Before, each group handled trouble in its own way, and the big fix was slow and scary. That did not work well for new places like chat rooms and code sites, so the club tried a new plan.
